A study conducted over a 10-year period focused on the surveillance of acute hepatitis C was published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2015 (Volume 20, Issue 1, Pages 89–97). 2. Talaat M, El-Sayed N, Kandeel A, Azab MA, Afifi S, Youssef FG, and colleagues conducted sentinel surveillance for patients with acute hepatitis in Egypt between 2001 and 2004. Their findings were published in the Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal in 2010 (Volume 16, Issue 2, Pages 134–140). 3. Tsatsralt-Od B, Takahashi M, Endo K, Buyankhuu O, Baatarkhuu O, Nishizawa T, and colleagues investigated infections with hepatitis A, B, C, and delta viruses among patients with acute hepatitis in Mongolia. Their research was published in the Journal of Medical Virology in 2006 (Volume 78, Issue 5, Pages 542–550). 4. Singh J, Bhatia R, Patnaik SK, Khare S, Bora D, Jain DC, and colleagues conducted community studies on hepatitis B in Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh, India, during 1997–1998. They identified unnecessary therapeutic injections as a major risk factor. This study was published in Epidemiology and Infection in 2000 (Volume 125, Issue 2, Pages 367–375). 5. Nelson NP authored a section on hepatitis A in the CDC Yellow Book 2018: Health Information for International Travel. This resource provides guidance on infectious diseases related to travel, including hepatitis A. The information was accessed on February 16, 2018. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines addressing ethical issues in public health surveillance. These guidelines are available online and were accessed on June 4, 2018. 7. A template case report form for acute viral hepatitis includes detailed patient identification, clinical characteristics, testing circumstances, and biomarker data. This form is designed to collect information on risk factors for acute hepatitis during the 2–6 weeks and 1–6 months prior to symptom onset. It is intended to be completed by healthcare workers after interviewing patients and reviewing medical records. 8. The surveillance system aims to identify the viruses responsible for acute hepatitis and trace the sources of infection. This information is used to improve prevention strategies and public health planning by the Ministry of Health. 9. Blood tests are proposed to determine the type of hepatitis (A, B, C, or E) a patient has. The results are securely stored in the patient’s medical records. If the patient consents, anonymized data may be used for surveillance purposes. 10. Risks associated with blood collection are minimal but may include discomfort, bleeding, bruising, swelling, fainting, or infection. Discussing personal circumstances during the interview may also cause discomfort. 11. Test results will be available at a specified time, and patients will need to return to the clinic to receive them. The results will guide further steps, including measures to protect others who may have been exposed to the virus, such as vaccination. 12. The benefits of participating include identifying the type of acute hepatitis, understanding how the infection occurred, and learning how to prevent future infections. Acute hepatitis generally does not require treatment, but patients should avoid unnecessary medications. 13. Patients have the right to refuse the use of their data for surveillance. If they decline, their data will remain confidential and will not be used for the project. This decision will not affect their care or access to test results. 14. Contact information is provided for patients to address any questions or concerns about the surveillance project or its ethical aspects. 15. WHO surveillance case definitions for viral hepatitis are designed for reporting and surveillance purposes. These definitions may differ from clinical management criteria. All symptoms must be present to diagnose acute hepatitis, and elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels are often used to improve specificity. 16. The West Haven Criteria for hepatic encephalopathy (HE) classify the condition into grades based on clinical and neuropsychological findings. These grades range from minimal HE (subtle psychometric or neurophysiological changes) to Grade IV HE (coma). The criteria emphasize the relationship between HE and liver insufficiency or portosystemic shunting. 17. The 2014 Practice Guideline on hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease, developed by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) and the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL), provides detailed diagnostic and management recommendations. This guideline was published in Hepatology in 2014 (Volume 60, Issue 2, Pages 715–735).
